name: Analyzing expert decision-making in geosteering: Statistical insights from a large-scale controlled experiment (Geosteering World Cup 2021, 349 participants) and related NORCE/UiS human-vs-machine studies
authors_org: Yasaman Cheraghi, Sergey Alyaev, Reidar B. Bratvold, Aojie Hong, Igor Kuvaev, Stephen Clark, Andrei Zhuravlev (University of Stavanger, NORCE Norwegian Research Centre, ROGII)
year: 2025 (journal); preceded by URTeC 2022 paper 'What Can We Learn After 10,000 Geosteering Decisions?' (URTeC-2022-3722510); dataset released 2025
venue_link: Applied Computing and Geosciences 2025: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2590197425000199 ; SSRN preprint: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4951357 ; URTeC 2022: https://onepetro.org/URTECONF/proceedings-abstract/22URTC/22URTC/D021S022R002/489183 ; JPT summary: https://jpt.spe.org/a-study-suggests-geosteers-often-are-missing-the-target ; Related robot benchmark (SPE J. 2025, doi 10.2118/218444-PA): https://onepetro.org/SJ/article/30/03/995/631101/Geosteering-Robot-Powered-by-Multiple
code_availability: Data public under CC-BY 4.0: Zenodo https://zenodo.org/records/15190744 (262 MB; JSON full player data following schema.json / schema_answer.json, plus CSV of interpolated interpretations per participant per step) and GitHub https://github.com/geosteering-no/10000-geosteering-interpretations-and-decisions (release 1.0). No analysis notebooks listed in the README.
evidence_level: Peer-reviewed (Applied Computing and Geosciences 2025) plus conference paper and trade-press summary; full text not accessible (HTTP 403), so findings are taken from abstracts, the Zenodo/GitHub records and the JPT summary.
extreme_summary: About 10,000 time-stamped interpretations and steering decisions from 349 experts in a controlled GWC 2021 simulation show large, inconsistent variation among experts using identical tools and data; interpretation quality is the main driver of good placement, misinterpretation (especially missed fault-induced shifts) is very costly, and only a small minority score well, so outcomes mix skill and luck.
task_definition: Humans interpret streaming LWD logs against a typewell using stratigraphy-based steering (SBS) in a ROGII cloud simulator, and every 2 minutes (per drilled segment) update their interpretation and choose the next bit target; scored on in-reservoir contact (target-zone footage), reservoir quality and drilling speed (JPT: zone contact 75%, ROP 25%).
inputs: Real-time lateral log (gamma ray) and trajectory, typewell / offset log, SBS interpretation tools (dip segments, faults) in a StarSteer-like cloud environment; true geomodels based on real fields with varying formation dips and faults; two wells (one conventional, one unconventional).
target_parameterisation: Human interpretations as SBS dip-segment models (sequence of segments with dips and fault throws) snapshotted over time; decisions as target positions / trajectory.
output_representation: Per-participant, per-step interpretation snapshots (interpolated to common steps in CSV) and trajectories; outcome scores per participant.
architecture: Not an ML method. Controlled experiment (competition) plus statistical analysis of correlation and causation between interpretation quality, decisions and well-placement scores; related work builds algorithmic baselines (particle filter + RL robot 'PluRaListic', earlier DSS-1) benchmarked against these humans.
core_mechanism: Using a single common synthetic truth with many independent human attempts makes it possible to separate interpretation skill, decision skill and luck. Findings reported: (1) interpretation quality is crucial and misinterpretation has a significant negative impact on placement; (2) faults cause large scoring drops because many participants missed fault-induced zone shifts; (3) a large fraction of participants passively followed the plan (177 excluded; about 24% actively geosteered), and active continuous steering helped; (4) the same individuals performed inconsistently across the two wells, and regional (North American) experience was not predictive; (5) interpretation errors did not always map to lower reservoir contact, i.e. decision quality and outcome are not linearly related under uncertainty; (6) authors attribute variability to the lack of unified guidelines for SBS decisions.
decoding: Humans commit to one interpretation per step (mode-seeking); no probabilistic hedging in SBS tools.
metric_consistent_decode: Humans are mode-seeking: they pick one band and steer to it. That is appropriate for an in-zone objective, not for pooled RMSE, where the posterior mean is optimal for a calibrated posterior.
evidence_scope: Whole lateral drilled so far plus typewell; sequential (causal) evidence only, no look-ahead, unlike our offline whole-lateral setting.
prefix_conditioning: Inherent: every new interpretation extends the participant's previous interpretation; errors made early persist (supports the 'one wrong pick propagates' practitioner view in A01).
propose_vs_select: Single human interpretation per step; the related PF+RL robot keeps hundreds of plausible interpretations (particles) and optimises decisions over them.
physical_constraints: SBS model: piecewise dips and fault throws relative to the typewell stratigraphy.
dataset: GWC 2021: 349 participants (JPT cites 329 scored), about 10,000 time-stamped interpretation+decision snapshots, two synthetic wells based on real fields with dips and faults, 2-minute decision cadence. CC-BY 4.0 on Zenodo/GitHub.
synthetic_to_real: Logs are synthetic, generated from truth geomodels built on real fields; no alignment stage relevant to ML training. The dataset could be used to build realistic hard cases (faults, dip changes) for our synthetic generator, and gives human interpretation traces over known truth.
metric_and_performance: JPT/URTeC summary: 50% of participants scored 30% or less; only 14 of 329 (4.3%) scored >= 60%. Related benchmarks: PF+RL robot (SPE J. 2025) median 77.3% reservoir contact over 1,000 runs, top 14% of GWC humans, best run above all humans; earlier study: DSS-1 algorithm beat 28 of 29 experts (arXiv 2005.08916, later withdrawn by authors); JPT cites a study where only 2 of 54 professionals outperformed uncertainty-based algorithms.
comparability: Not comparable to TVT RMSE: scores are in-zone contact and ROP. Qualitatively, it establishes that human TVT interpretation of repeated/faulted stratigraphy is itself noisy, which bounds label quality if labels come from human interpretations. [uncertain]
validation_protocol: Controlled experiment with common truth; statistical correlation/causation analysis. Details of tests not verified (full text inaccessible).
inference_budget: Humans: 2-minute decision interval under time pressure; not relevant to our compute budget.
repeated_layers: Main human failure is misinterpretation of geological features, notably missing fault-induced shifts, which in TVT space look like jumping to a different repeated band. Humans lack probabilistic hedging, so a wrong band choice becomes a persistent error. No specific tie-breaking protocol was found; the authors emphasise that no unified guideline exists.
drift: Not specifically analysed in the accessible material. Dip misestimation (slow drift) is implied by the dip-varying truth models, but no quantitative breakdown was found. [uncertain]
uncertainty_and_calibration: Human interpretations are single-valued, without uncertainty; the paper's point is that decisions should account for uncertainty. The related robot uses particle-filter multi-interpretation (hundreds of hypotheses) and outperforms most humans, supporting calibrated multi-hypothesis outputs.
where_to_use: (1) Label-noise prior: if Kaggle TVT labels come from human interpretations, there is an irreducible label noise and systematic fault/band picking bias; use this to set expectations and to consider robust losses near faults. (2) Synthetic data: human trace data and fault-heavy truth models can inform harder synthetic cases (faults as abrupt band shifts). (3) Evaluation: split holdout RMSE by presence of fault-like jumps in the label to see whether our band-confusion errors concentrate there. (4) Justification for a calibrated multi-hypothesis posterior over single-path decoding.
error_mode_targeted: Band confusion (~51%), especially the fault-induced subset; secondarily measurement/protocol (label noise from human interpretation).
gap_vs_our_implementation: Experts do not have cues that our model lacks in the Kaggle setting: they see the same GR, trajectory and typewell, only causally, and they score poorly on average, whereas our model sees the full lateral and outputs a distribution. The cues they rely on that we may under-use are structural: fault-aware reinterpretation (explicit vertical jumps), segment-wise dip consistency, and prefix continuity. Our gaps: (a) no explicit analysis of error vs fault-like label jumps; (b) no explicit fault/jump modelling in the output (per-column softmax can represent jumps, but no loss/prior encourages 'smooth with rare jumps'); (c) synthetic generator may under-represent faults (85% synthetic training) [uncertain]; (d) we have not quantified label noise, which human-variability evidence suggests is non-trivial. We already do: whole-lateral evidence, distributional output with expectation decode (the robot study's lesson that multi-hypothesis beats single-path is consistent with our design).
proposed_experiment: E1 (analysis, CPU, low): in posterior_analysis.py, detect fault-like jumps in holdout labels (|dTVT/dMD - local dip trend| above a threshold, or piecewise-linear fit residual jumps) and report the share of squared error within +-N columns after jumps vs elsewhere, for the 155 holdout wells. If band-confusion error concentrates after jumps, prioritise fault-aware synthetic data. E2 (data, medium): add fault throws (random vertical offsets at random MD, magnitude matched to typical layer thickness, i.e. a jump to an adjacent repeated band) to the synthetic well generator used for the 85% synthetic portion; 60-epoch ConvNeXt with and without, 2 seeds, compare pooled RMSE and the wrong_mode component. E3 (label-noise estimate, low): on training wells, measure disagreement between label TVT and the best piecewise-linear refit, and check whether GWC human interpretation spread (from the Zenodo CSVs, where truth is known) gives a realistic human error scale; use this as the floor for expectations.
implementation_effort: E1 low (analysis on existing dumps); E2 medium (generator change + retrain); E3 low-medium (download 262 MB CC-BY data, parse JSON/CSV).
gpu_cost: E1/E3: none. E2: one 60-epoch ConvNeXt run per seed per arm on the RTX 5060 8 GB (a few hours each). [uncertain]
distillation_compatibility: E2 changes teacher training data only; KD on posteriors to FastViT unaffected. E1/E3 are analysis.
error_correlation_with_ours: Not a model; no blend member. Human interpretations are a different error source (causal, single-path) and are not available at test time.
risk: The GWC study measures steering outcomes, not TVT accuracy, and its findings about humans may not transfer to an offline, whole-lateral ML setting. GWC wells are synthetic from two field-based geomodels, so statistics may not represent the Kaggle distribution. Full text was not accessible; specific statistical effects (e.g. effect sizes for interpretation quality, skill vs luck split) are unverified. Adding faults to synthetic data can hurt if Kaggle holdout wells rarely contain faults.
notes: Related NORCE line (see A05/A07): 'An interactive sequential-decision benchmark from geosteering' (Alyaev et al., ACAGS 2021, arXiv 2011.00733) and the withdrawn 'Man vs machine' (arXiv 2005.08916). ROGII GWC runs annually (GWC 2024, GWC 2026 pages on rogii.com), so newer human-performance data may appear. The dataset records human interpretations over a known truth, which in principle allows measuring human TVT RMSE directly -- a useful sanity reference for our 4.7-4.8 ft numbers, if units and geometry are comparable. [uncertain]
